concepts.title: Components and JSX
concepts.description: React lets you describe UI declaratively as a tree of components (plain functions that return JSX, which is syntactic sugar for calling React.createElement) instead of manually mutating the DOM.
learningObjectives: Explain why React favors declarative UI over manual DOM manipulation.
Define what a React component is.
Explain that JSX is not HTML, but syntactic sugar for React.createElement calls.
Explain why props are read-only and what that means for how components communicate.
Write a simple functional component that accepts and renders props.

sections.heading: Why React Exists: Declarative vs Imperative UI
sections.body:
Before frameworks like React, building an interactive UI with plain JavaScript meant writing **imperative** code: you manually call `document.createElement`, set `.textContent` or `.className`, call `.appendChild`, and later, whenever the underlying data changes, you have to remember every place in the DOM that needs to be found again and updated to match. This works for small examples but scales badly: as an app grows, update logic ends up scattered everywhere, and the DOM easily drifts out of sync with your data, because keeping them in sync is your job, by hand, every time.

React's core idea is **declarative** UI: instead of writing the steps to mutate the DOM, you write a function that describes *what the UI should look like right now, given the current data*, and you describe it again on every change rather than patching the previous result. React takes your description (a tree of elements) and, using an internal 'diffing' process (reconciliation), works out the minimal set of real DOM changes needed to match it. You stop asking 'how do I mutate the DOM from state A to state B' and ask 'what does the UI look like for this state,' which is much easier to reason about and test as an application grows.

sections.heading: What Is a Component?
JSX Is Not HTML
Props: Read-Only Inputs to a Component
sections.body:
**Props** (short for 'properties') are how a parent component passes data down into a child component, much like arguments passed into a function. `<Greeting name="Amara" />` leads React to call `Greeting({ name: "Amara" })`; inside `Greeting`, `props.name` (or, more commonly, a destructured parameter, `function Greeting({ name }) { ... }`) gives you that value.

The rule to learn early: **a component must never mutate its own props.** Treat props as read-only, the way you treat a function's parameters as inputs you read, not values you reassign and expect the caller to notice. Writing `props.count = props.count + 1` inside a component doesn't do what it looks like it does: React has no way of knowing you changed something, so the screen doesn't update, and you've broken the component's contract with its parent, which owns that data and never authorized the child to change it. (In development builds React also freezes the props object, so in strict-mode code that assignment throws a TypeError.) If a component needs to display something that changes over time in response to user interaction, it needs its own **state** (covered in a later concept). State is what a component owns and can update itself; props are what a parent hands down and the child only reads. This one-way flow of data, parent to child, keeps large React applications easier to trace and debug, because a value's origin can always be followed up the component tree instead of being mutated from arbitrary places.

Since a component is a function, any nested function you define inside it, such as an event handler, follows the closure rules from the JavaScript Foundations module. A handler defined inside a component closes over that particular call's props (and, later, state), which is part of why closures are worth understanding before React.

examples.title: Imperative DOM Update vs a Declarative Component
examples.explanation: The imperative version has to clear out old content, create a new button, set its text, wire up a click handler, and re-insert it, and it has to get every step right each time count changes, or the UI falls out of sync with the real count. The declarative Counter component does none of that DOM bookkeeping: it describes 'a button that shows this count and calls onIncrement when clicked' for whatever count currently is. React works out how to update the real DOM to match that description each time the component is called again with new props. You never call document.createElement or .appendChild yourself.

examples.title: JSX Compiles to React.createElement
examples.explanation: `element` and `sameElement` describe the same thing: an h1 element with a className attribute and text content built from a literal string plus the value of `name`. The `{name}` inside the JSX is not a string but a JavaScript expression slot, which is why a variable, a function call, or a ternary all work there. This shows JSX is not HTML parsed by the browser: it's a nicer way to write calls to a regular JavaScript function, resolved by the build tool before any browser sees the code.

examples.title: A Simple Component That Accepts Props
examples.explanation:
Greeting takes props (destructured directly in the parameter list into `name` and `isNewUser`, instead of writing `props.name` everywhere) and returns a description of a div containing a heading and a conditional paragraph. `{isNewUser &&

...

}` is a common JSX idiom for conditional rendering: if isNewUser is false, the && short-circuits to false, and React renders nothing for a false/null/undefined child; if it's true, the && evaluates to the JSX on the right, which gets rendered. The parent decides the values of name and isNewUser; Greeting only reads them, which is the read-only contract props are meant to enforce.

misconceptions.description: JSX is basically HTML that you're allowed to write directly inside your JavaScript files.
misconceptions.clarification: JSX only looks like HTML. It compiles (via a build tool like Babel) into nested React.createElement(type, props, children) function calls before it reaches a browser; browsers never execute JSX directly. This is why JSX has rules HTML doesn't: attribute names are camelCase (className, onClick) rather than HTML's class and onclick; any value inside { } is evaluated as a JavaScript expression, not treated as text; tags without children must self-close (); and a compile step is always required, since no browser natively understands JSX.
misconceptions.fact: JSX only looks like HTML. It compiles (via a build tool like Babel) into nested React.createElement(type, props, children) function calls before it reaches a browser; browsers never execute JSX directly.

misconceptions.description: You can update what's displayed by directly changing a prop inside the component, e.g. props.count = props.count + 1.
misconceptions.clarification: Props are meant to be read-only from the receiving component's perspective; they're owned and controlled by the parent that passed them down. Mutating props.count directly doesn't trigger a re-render (React only re-renders in response to state changes or new props arriving from a parent), and it breaks the component's contract with its parent, which has no idea its data was changed. (In development builds the assignment even throws, because React freezes the props object.) If a component needs to display a value that changes over time, it needs its own local state (introduced later, via the useState hook). State is what a component owns and can update itself; props are an input the component only reads.
misconceptions.fact: Props are meant to be read-only from the receiving component's perspective; they're owned and controlled by the parent that passed them down.

exercises.prompt: Given this component, what does each of the two calls below actually return when called directly as plain JavaScript functions (not rendered by React)?
hints: Badge is a JavaScript function. Calling it directly (outside of JSX/React) gives you back whatever its return statement evaluates to, nothing more.
What does the ternary `count > 0 ? ... : null` evaluate to when count is 0, versus when count is 3?
Remember that JSX compiles to React.createElement(...) calls, which return plain JavaScript objects describing an element, not strings and not anything drawn on a screen.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The first call returns null, since count > 0 is false when count is 0. The second call returns a React element object describing a <span> whose children are the label, ': ', and the count (3). It is not a string, and calling Badge() directly like this doesn't render anything; it only produces that description.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Badge is an ordinary JavaScript function, and calling it directly like this evaluates its body and returns whatever the return statement produces; React isn't involved. With count: 0, `count > 0` is false, so the ternary evaluates to `null`, which is what gets logged. With count: 3, `count > 0` is true, so the ternary evaluates the JSX `{label}: {count}`, which, because JSX is sugar for React.createElement, produces a plain JavaScript object describing a span element, not a string and not anything visibly rendered. Only when such an element is handed to React (via ReactDOM's createRoot/render APIs, or returned from a component in a mounted tree) does it become real DOM nodes on screen.

exercises.prompt: This component is supposed to let the user increment a displayed count by clicking the button, but clicking it never changes what's shown on screen (assume it's rendered by React, and React only re-renders a component when its state or props change). Find the bug and describe the fix.
hints: count is a prop here, not a variable this component can reassign and expect anything to react to.
Even if `count = count + 1` runs without crashing and console.log shows an increasing number, does React know this component's inputs changed, so that it would re-render?
A component that needs to own a value which changes over time in response to user interaction needs its own state (e.g. via useState), not a mutated prop.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is that `count` is a prop, an input owned by the parent, and the component tries to change it with `count = count + 1`. That reassignment only changes the local `count` variable for that one render's handler; it doesn't notify React that anything changed, so React never re-renders the button, and it violates the rule that a component must not mutate its own props. console.log(count) can still show the value climbing inside that one function call, which is what makes the bug easy to miss: something is happening, just nothing that affects the screen. The fix is to give the component its own state with the useState hook (covered in the next part of the course): `useState(initialCount)` gives the component a `count` value it owns plus a `setCount` function, and calling `setCount(...)` tells React to re-render the component with the new value. The prop is renamed to `initialCount` to show it only seeds the state once, instead of being something the component keeps reading or mutating.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best describes what JSX actually is?
options: A templating language, similar to Handlebars or Mustache, that generates an HTML string at runtime.
A special dialect of HTML that browsers can parse and render natively, once inside a .jsx file.
A CSS-in-JS system for styling React components.
A syntax extension that a build tool compiles into nested React.createElement(type, props, children) calls; browsers never receive or execute JSX directly.
assessments.explanation: JSX is a syntax extension to JavaScript, compiled ahead of time (typically by Babel) into ordinary JavaScript function calls, nested calls to React.createElement, before the code reaches a browser. The “A special dialect of HTML that browsers…” option is wrong because no browser understands JSX natively, whatever the file extension; a compile step is always required. The “A templating language, similar to Handlebars…” option is wrong because JSX doesn't produce an HTML string. It produces JavaScript objects describing elements, a more structured representation that React's reconciliation process works on directly. The “A CSS-in-JS system for styling React components” option confuses JSX with an unrelated category of styling tools.

assessments.prompt: Explain to someone who has only built websites with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript why React describes UI 'declaratively,' and what problem that solves compared to manually updating the DOM.
assessments.modelAnswer: When you build UI with plain JavaScript, you write imperative code: explicit, ordered instructions like document.createElement, element.textContent = ..., element.appendChild(...), that mutate the DOM step by step. The catch is that your code becomes responsible for keeping the DOM in sync with your data at every point where that data can change, and as an app grows there are more places where you must remember to update the right DOM nodes by hand, in the right order, without missing one. The screen easily drifts out of sync with your data, because keeping them matched is manual, error-prone bookkeeping spread across the codebase. React's declarative approach flips this: instead of writing the steps to mutate the DOM from its old state to its new state, you write a function (a component) that describes what the UI should look like right now, for the current data, and you describe it again, fresh, every time the data changes. React takes that description (a tree of elements, usually written with JSX), compares it to the previous one, and applies only the minimal real DOM changes needed to match, a process called reconciliation. You stop tracking 'what DOM mutations get me from the old screen to the new one' and answer only 'what does the UI look like for this data,' a simpler and more predictable question as the application and its state grow.

assessments.prompt: What is the core problem with the imperative approach to building UI as an application grows?
options: It cannot make use of JavaScript closures at all.
Browsers execute imperative DOM code more slowly than they execute declarative code.
Update logic ends up scattered across the codebase.
It requires too many CSS classes to stay organized.
assessments.explanation: The core argument against imperative UI code isn't about performance or syntax. Manually calling document.createElement, .textContent, and .appendChild means your code, not a framework, must find and update every affected DOM node each time the data changes. As an app grows, that responsibility is scattered across more places, and the real DOM easily drifts out of sync with the data. Declarative UI (describing what the UI should look like for the current data and letting React work out the DOM changes via reconciliation) removes that bookkeeping burden; it isn't meant to make code run faster or to reduce CSS.

assessments.prompt:
A component is defined as `function greeting(props) { return

Hi, {props.name}

; }` (a lowercase name) and used in JSX as ``. What actually happens?
options: React renders it correctly by calling greeting({ name: "Amara" }), since JSX doesn't care about capitalization.
JSX compiles <greeting /> as a literal, built-in tag named "greeting" (like <div> or <span>).
It throws a compile-time SyntaxError immediately, because component names must be capitalized.
React automatically capitalizes the tag internally before rendering, so it still works exactly as intended.
assessments.explanation: JSX distinguishes a component reference from a literal HTML/DOM tag by capitalization: a lowercase tag name compiles to a string tag name passed to React.createElement (the same treatment <div> or <span> get), while a capitalized name compiles to a reference to that identifier, which React calls as a function. Since greeting starts lowercase, <greeting /> is treated as an unrecognized built-in element called "greeting", and the greeting function is never invoked. There's no SyntaxError (“It throws a compile-time SyntaxError immediately…”) and no automatic fix-up (“React automatically capitalizes the tag internally before…”); you just get the wrong output, typically with a console warning that the tag is unrecognized.

options: className={...} needs curly braces without surrounding quotes.
className must always be a hardcoded string; conditional classes require a separate CSS-in-JS library to work at all.
Nothing -- this correctly applies the "active" class whenever isActive is true.
JSX attributes cannot contain ternary expressions under any syntax.
assessments.explanation: In JSX, { } with no surrounding quotes marks an attribute value as a JavaScript expression to be evaluated rather than a literal string. Here the whole expression, braces included, is inside double quotes, which makes it one literal string; React never evaluates isActive ? 'active' : '', and className ends up set to the useless text "{isActive ? 'active' : ''}". The fix is to remove the surrounding quotes: className={isActive ? "active" : ""}. Ternaries work fine inside a correctly-written {} expression slot, ruling out the “JSX attributes cannot contain ternary expressions under any syntax” option, and no separate library is required, ruling out the “className must always be a hardcoded string…” option.

assessments.prompt: In plain HTML, `` is perfectly valid on its own, with no closing tag or self-close needed. What happens if you write that exact same markup inside JSX?
options: React silently ignores the img tag entirely and renders nothing in its place.

It's a syntax error -- JSX requires every tag to either be self-closed () or have an explicit matching closing tag, since JSX has no concept of certain tags being inherently childless the way HTML does.
It compiles without any error, but the image itself never actually appears on screen.
It works identically to HTML, since JSX is just HTML embedded directly inside JavaScript.
assessments.explanation: JSX is not HTML. It's syntax that compiles to nested React.createElement calls, and that compilation has no notion of certain elements (like img, br, or input) being childless, as HTML's parser does. JSX therefore requires every element to say whether it has children: either self-close it () or give it a closing tag. An unclosed as plain HTML allows is a compile-time syntax error in JSX, not a silently ignored case.

Nothing -- React happily renders multiple sibling elements returned directly like this.
tags are not allowed to appear as a direct child of a component's return statement.

options: The price updates exactly once, on the second click, then stops changing.
The displayed price visibly decreases by 10% with each click, exactly as the code seems to intend.
React throws a runtime TypeError the first time applyDiscount runs, since props are frozen, immutable objects.
The displayed price never visibly changes.
assessments.explanation: price is a prop, an input owned by PriceTag's parent, and price = price * 0.9 only reassigns a local variable (the destructured parameter) inside the component; it calls no React API and gives React no signal that something changed. Since nothing tells React to re-render, the span keeps showing the price it was rendered with, on every click, even though the reassignment runs without error each time. It runs without error because it rebinds a local variable rather than writing to the props object, so there is nothing to throw, which rules out the “React throws a runtime TypeError the first…” option. To show a value that visibly updates, the component has to own it as state via useState and call the setter, not reassign a prop.

options: Avatar(["pic.png", "Amara"]) -- the attributes become an array in the order they're written.
Avatar(document.querySelector("Avatar")) -- React looks up the element in the DOM first.
Avatar({ url: "pic.png", name: "Amara" }) -- every attribute is collected into a single object and passed as one argument.
Avatar("pic.png", "Amara") -- each attribute becomes its own positional argument.
assessments.explanation: However many attributes a JSX element has, they're gathered into one props object and passed as a single argument to the component function, the same mechanism that makes <Greeting name="Amara" /> call Greeting({ name: "Amara" }). Avatar receives one object, { url: "pic.png", name: "Amara" }, and reads props.url and props.name from it. That's why destructuring the props parameter in the signature, function Avatar({ url, name }), is so common: it destructures the one object argument, not several positional arguments.

options: The literal text "0" is rendered inside the div.
"0 items" is rendered, since itemCount is still technically a valid, defined number.
React throws an error, since 0 cannot be used as the left operand of the && operator in JSX.
Nothing is rendered -- the div appears empty.
assessments.explanation: && evaluates its left operand and, if it's falsy, returns that value without evaluating the right side. 0 is falsy, so itemCount && ... evaluates to the number 0, not to false or null. React skips rendering only for false, null, and undefined children; a number like 0 is a valid, renderable child, so React renders it as the text "0". This is a well-known pitfall of the && conditional-rendering idiom: it renders nothing only for booleans/null/undefined, not for every falsy value, so an itemCount of 0 shows a stray "0" instead of hiding the badge. Comparing explicitly (itemCount > 0 && ...) avoids it.

options: Header is treated as a plain, unrecognized DOM tag named "Header", since it appears in JSX without explicitly being called like a function.
React ends up calling Header() (with an empty props object) as part of rendering the tree Page returns.
Page must explicitly write Header() itself somewhere in its own function body for Header's output to show up.
Header never actually runs at all -- <Header /> is just a static label, so "My App" would need to be hardcoded separately inside Page for it to appear on screen.
assessments.explanation: Because Header is capitalized, JSX compiles <Header /> into a createElement call that references the Header identifier (rather than a string tag name), and React calls that function while resolving the tree Page returns, with an empty props object. This is the 'components compose like functions, and an app is a tree of components calling other components' model: Page doesn't call Header() itself (ruling out the “Page must explicitly write Header() itself somewhere…” option); referencing it in JSX is what makes React call it. The “Header is treated as a plain, unrecognized…” option describes what would happen only if the name were lowercase, and the “Header never actually runs at all…” option ignores that JSX component references are live calls, not static labels.
